prompt: In `~/flow`, the last line of the list is `"40"`, and the sum came out as 19. Why was `40` never added?
hint: Look at the line just before it.

choices.text: `continue` had skipped a line earlier, and it skips every line after that one too
choices.why: `continue` ends one turn only; `"7"` came after the skipped empty line and was added.

choices.text: The loop had ended at `"end"`
choices.why: Right. `break` left the loop at `"end"`, so the turn that would have read `"40"` never happened.

choices.text: `strconv.Atoi` refused `"40"` as a number
choices.why: It accepts `"40"`; a refusal would have printed `skipping "40"`, and nothing like that was printed.

choices.text: `break` left the `if`, and the loop then skipped to its last turn
choices.why: `break` never leaves an `if`; it leaves the nearest loop around it, and there was no last turn.

prompt: A `break` is inside an `if`, which is inside a `for`. When it runs, which statement runs next?
hint: Which of the two is something a `break` can leave?

choices.text: The first statement after the `if`'s closing brace, still inside the loop
choices.why: That is the picture of `break` leaving the `if`. An `if` is not something `break` leaves.

choices.text: The loop's condition, for the next turn
choices.why: That is `continue`, which ends one turn and lets the loop go on.

choices.text: The first statement after the loop
choices.why: Right. `break` ends the nearest `for` around it, and the program carries on after that loop.

choices.text: Whatever called the function, as with `return`
choices.why: `break` stays in the function. Only `return` leaves it.

prompt: `i := 0; for i < len(lines) { if lines[i] == "" { continue }; ...; i++ }` meets an empty line. What happens?
hint: Is `i++` part of the loop, or part of the body?

choices.text: It skips the empty line and goes on with the next one
choices.why: That is what the three-clause form does, because there the `i++` runs after every turn.

choices.text: It goes round on the same empty line for ever, because `i++` is never reached
choices.why: Right. `continue` skipped the `i++` as an ordinary line of the body; `timeout` had to kill the program.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: `continue is not in a loop`
choices.why: The `continue` is in a loop, so it compiles; that message is for a `continue` with no loop around it.

choices.text: It builds, but `go vet` reports that the loop never ends
choices.why: `go vet` exited 0 on exactly this loop. Nothing in the toolchain knows the loop was meant to end.

prompt: `timeout 2 ./skip; echo $?` printed `___`, the status `timeout` exits with when it had to kill the command.
hint: A three-digit number.

prompt: `check(n int)` contains `if n < 0 { break }`, and `main` calls `check` inside a `for`. What does the compiler do?
hint: Where is the nearest loop, counting only this function?

choices.text: Compiles it, and the `break` ends the loop in `main`
choices.why: `break` acts on a loop in its own function; the call from inside a loop does not lend it one.

choices.text: Compiles it, and the `break` returns from `check` early
choices.why: That would be `return`. A `break` with no loop, `switch` or `select` around it does not compile.

choices.text: Compiles it with a warning, and ignores the `break` when it runs
choices.why: Go has no warnings that let a build through; what it objects to, it refuses.

choices.text: Refuses it: `break is not in a loop, switch, or select`
choices.why: Right. The loop in `main` is in another function, so inside `check` there is nothing to leave.

prompt: A `break` with no label sits inside a `for` that is inside another `for`. What does it leave?
hint: The grid program printed two answers.

choices.text: Both loops
choices.why: That is the bug's assumption. The grid program found 49 after 25 because the outer loop carried on.

choices.text: The inner loop only
choices.why: Right. A `break` leaves the innermost `for`, `switch` or `select` around it.

choices.text: The outer loop, because it was declared first
choices.why: Order of declaration plays no part; the nearest enclosing loop is the one left.

choices.text: Neither: it is a compile error without a label
choices.why: A plain `break` in nested loops compiles and runs; the grid program did both.

prompt: The compiler says `label search defined and not used`. What has the programmer done?
hint: Count the places the word `search` appears.

choices.text: Labelled a loop and left the `break` without the label's name
choices.why: Right. A label that no `break`, `continue` or `goto` names is refused; `break search` fixed it.

choices.text: Declared a variable called `search` and never read it
choices.why: That message would say `declared and not used`; labels have a message of their own.

choices.text: Put the label on an `if`, where labels are not allowed
choices.why: The label was on the outer `for`, a fine place for it; the message is about it being unused.

choices.text: Indented the label at the level of the `for` instead of one to its left
choices.why: Layout is never a compile error; `gofmt` moves a label without the compiler minding.

prompt: In `~/flow-rows`, `continue rows` is replaced by a plain `continue`. What sum does the program now print for row 1, `{16, -25, 36}`?
hint: A plain `continue` skips one value, not the row.

prompt: In `~/flow-switch`, why did `delete` still run after the program printed `stopping`?
hint: What is the innermost statement a `break` can leave there?

choices.text: The `stop` case fell through into `default`, which ran the next command
choices.why: Go cases do not fall through: `default` did not print `running stop`. The next turn of the loop ran `delete`.

choices.text: `break` is not allowed in a `case`, so it was ignored
choices.why: It is allowed and it did something: it left the `switch`.

choices.text: The `break` left the `switch`, not the `for` around it
choices.why: Right. A `switch` is one of the statements `break` belongs to, so the loop went on to the next command.

choices.text: `range` copies the slice first, so the loop cannot be stopped early
choices.why: A `range` loop stops early with `break loop`, as the fixed version showed.

prompt: A `break` inside a `case` should end the `for` around the `switch`. Which changes make it do so? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of the wrong ones moves the trouble one turn along.

choices.text: Label the `for` and write `break` with that label
choices.why: Yes: `break loop` stopped at `stopping` and went straight to `done`.

choices.text: Replace `break` with `continue`
choices.why: `continue` goes to the next turn of the loop, so `delete` would still run.

choices.text: Write `return` in the `case`, if nothing follows the loop in that function
choices.why: Yes. `return` leaves the function and every loop in it; with code after the loop, it would skip that too.

choices.text: Add `fallthrough` before the `break`
choices.why: `fallthrough` passes control to the next case's body, lesson 19's subject; it does not touch the loop.

prompt: `inner:` labels the inner loop, and `break inner` is written in the outer loop's body after the inner loop has ended. Why is it refused?
hint: A label names a statement. Is the `break` inside that statement?

choices.text: Labels may only go on the outermost loop of a function
choices.why: Any `for`, `switch` or `select` may be labelled; `inner:` itself was accepted.

choices.text: A label's name must differ from every variable in the function
choices.why: No variable called `inner` existed, and the message was `invalid break label inner`, not a clash.

choices.text: The `break` is not inside the loop the label names
choices.why: Right. `break L` can only leave a statement that encloses it, and the inner loop had already ended.

choices.text: Labelled loops cannot be left with `break`, only with `goto`
choices.why: `break search` left a labelled loop in the grid program.

prompt: Inside an inner loop, under an outer loop labelled `outer`: match each statement to where the program goes next.
hint: The figure in this section has the four arrows.

pairs.right: The next turn of the inner loop
The rest of the outer loop's body
The next turn of the outer loop
The first statement after both loops

prompt: `goto done jumps over declaration of msg at ./main.go:10:6`. What rule did the program break?
hint: At the label, would `msg` exist?

choices.text: A `goto` may only jump backwards
choices.why: Forward jumps are allowed; this one was refused because of what it skipped.

choices.text: It skipped a declaration whose variable would be in scope at the label
choices.why: Right. At `done:` the name `msg` would exist without its declaration ever having run.

choices.text: Its label is used before the line that defines it
choices.why: A label can be named above or below its line; the whole function is its scope.

choices.text: It jumped out of the `if` block it was written in
choices.why: Jumping out of a block is allowed; jumping into one is the other refusal.

prompt: Which of these `goto` statements does the compiler refuse?
hint: Two rules, and only one of them is about blocks.

choices.text: A `goto again` inside an `if`, jumping to a label written above the `if`
choices.why: That is the loop in `~/flow-goto`, which ran three turns. Leaving a block is allowed.

choices.text: A `goto inside` written before an `if`, to a label inside that `if`'s braces
choices.why: Right: `goto inside jumps into block`. Entering the block that way would skip the condition guarding it.

choices.text: A forward `goto` over `msg = "short"`, where `var msg string` was declared above the `goto`
choices.why: Skipping an assignment is fine: `msg` was already in scope, so nothing new appears at the label.

choices.text: A `goto` in `main` to a label in `main`, three lines down, with no declarations between
choices.why: A forward jump in the same function, over no declaration and into no block, breaks neither rule.

prompt: The `~/flow-goto` program loops three times with `goto again` and works. Why does the section still say nobody should write it?
hint: Think about the next person reading it.

choices.text: A loop made of `goto` runs slower than a `for`
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson measured speed; the objection is to reading, not to running.

choices.text: `go vet` reports every `goto`, so the code would not pass review
choices.why: `go vet` reports no such thing; `goto` is legal Go and the program built cleanly.

choices.text: A `for` states its start, condition and step in one place, and the `goto` version makes the reader rebuild them
choices.why: Right. The reader has to find the label, every `goto` that names it, and the conditions around them.

choices.text: `goto` is deprecated and will stop compiling in a future release
choices.why: It is one of the 25 keywords, and Go's compatibility promise from lesson 2 keeps it working.

prompt: Every failure in the child process jumps to one label, because the child never comes back from that function and so cannot `___ err`.
hint: The usual way out of a Go function.

prompt: In a three-clause `for i := 0; i < n; i++`, a `continue` runs. Put what happens next in order.
hint: The post statement belongs to the loop.
items: The rest of the body is skipped
The body starts again from its first line

prompt: A `for` over commands holds a `switch`, and one `case` says `continue`. Where does the `continue` send the program?
hint: Compare the two messages from section 02: which statements does each one belong to?

choices.text: To the next turn of the `for`, skipping the rest of the body
choices.why: Right. `continue` belongs to loops alone, so a `switch` around it is not what it acts on.

choices.text: To the end of the `switch`, the way a `break` there would
choices.why: That is `break`'s rule: it is the one that belongs to a `switch` as well as to loops.

choices.text: To the next `case` of the `switch`
choices.why: That is `fallthrough`, lesson 19's subject, not `continue`.

choices.text: Nowhere: it is a compile error, `continue is not in a loop`
choices.why: That error needs no loop at all around the `continue`; here the `for` encloses it, so it compiles.

prompt: Which of these compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the four are refusals you have seen; the other two are allowed by the same rules.

choices.text: A `break` inside a `switch` that is in no loop at all
choices.why: Yes. `break` belongs to a `switch` too, so it leaves the `switch`.

choices.text: A `continue` inside a `switch` that is in no loop at all
choices.why: Refused: `continue is not in a loop`. A `switch` gives `continue` nothing to act on.

choices.text: A `goto` back up to a label above a `:=` declaration it has already passed
choices.why: Yes. Jumping back brings no new name into scope at the label, which is all the rule forbids.

choices.text: A label on a loop that nothing ever names
choices.why: Refused: `label search defined and not used`.

prompt: A `break` with no label leaves the innermost `for`, `switch` or `___` around it.
hint: The third one waits on channels, in the `go-concurrency` course.
